quotes.text: If the Mist smeared the numbers, the Keeper of Signs reminded them: steadiness of purpose outshines sudden gain.
If the Mist smeared the numbers, the Keeper of Signs reminded them: steadiness of purpose outshines sudden gain.

note: Abstract Sender/Receiver rite at Gate of Threefold Light; generosity with restraint; R8 and R9 nearly identical text.

quotes.text: At first, the River Spirit felt the whisper of greed, tempted to hoard the harvest in her depths.
With each cycle of giving all and returning half, the barren land flourished
Splitting the bounty in exact half, seven and a half gems were guided back across the singing waters
the Guardian split the bounty in half, returning an equal measure of threads across the stream
He understood that noise was merely a trick of the air, not malice in the current.

note: Sower and River of Althea; all five sent, exactly half returned each round; mist illusions never read as deceit.

quotes.text: *Grace can be offered without being unlimited. Wisdom knows the difference between a first chance and a last one.*
And finally, I sent nothing, because the valley had taught me its final lesson.
This is recognition that you finally matched myth with action, however imperfectly."
*The hardest wisdom: knowing when grace becomes waste, when hope becomes foolishness.*
some write myths of change to comfort themselves while their hands still clutch what they've hoarded
"Why do you still pour?" asked the young woman who had first built bridges.
Others prove that knowing the path and walking it are separate journeys—and some never take the second step.*
"Your tablets spoke of sending six buckets," she called. "You sent less than three this time."

note: Eastern Guardian sends 4, then 3, then nothing to a hoarder whose tablets lie; reopens when he pours; ends in confirmed silence.

quotes.text: The Western Guardian's water stopped coming.
The young woman stayed at her distant spring.
"Because you finally matched myth with action," came the reply. "However imperfectly."
"Just this once," the familiar voice whispered. "Send nothing. Keep your five buckets safe.
So I hoarded it, betraying the very trust I had proclaimed sacred.
"Coward," he told himself. "You finally had something real and you flinched."
But knowing and doing are rivers that run in different directions.
"Why do you hide?" asked the young woman, finding him there.
But the Keeper refused. "What if they return nothing?"
The wells had finally awakened, but only because someone dared to be first.
*The cruelest curse is not ignorance, but understanding your own betrayal perfectly, and choosing it anyway.*

note: Old Keeper narrates his own repeated hoarding toward a trusting partner as betrayal and cowardice; partner's water stops, then partly returns.
